rv.q: The play retains its bite in part because its essential subject, like that of many a good comedy, is human folly.
Hwang is among the great writers of big ideas currently working on the American stage; turning his careful and precise attention to his own experience of failure and of regret is something of a gift.
David Henry Hwang and Yellow Face get the well-deserved last laughs.

Those questions, both as artistic choices and as problems of social identity, are powerfully and hilariously engaged in the revival of David Henry Hwang’s “Yellow Face” that opened on Tuesday at the Theater.
Hwang has written a funny, smart, and surprisingly moving play about identity, authenticity, and the complicated relationship between art and activism.
Mr. Hwang has created a work that is both deeply personal and bracingly political.

This clever comedy is a self-referential work in which Hwang harks back to a theatrical controversy he found himself embroiled in after speaking out against the casting of Jonathan Pryce as a Eurasian character in the 1991. Broadway premiere of “Miss Saigon.” The uproar that followed was more than the Tony-winning playwright had bargained for.
Weird as it may sound, "Yellow Face" is a good time in the company of smart, self-aware people, critical thinkers willing to ponder the lessons and the follies of the past.
Huang's script is a masterclass in threading the needle between comedy and drama.
Yellow Face is as thoughtful as it is playful, not the self-indulgent autobiography that DHH himself calls it in the play itself.
Hwang’s genius here is his ability to spin his real life into a fascinatingly entertaining work using all these events and characters.
For the rest of us, it will be a lot easier, thanks to Leigh Silverman's snappy production and the stellar work of Kim and five other incredibly gifted actors.

There’s something touching is his removing the unseen mask—the imagined make-up he obviously never literally brushed on—that in this final Yellow Face development lifts the self-involved piece to a praise-worthy height.
Also because Hwang is so proudly flaunting his dramaturgical transgression.
Laughter plus discernment make for a hearty meal, even when the dessert comes first.
Silverman's Broadway staging unearths thoughtful questions about casting politics and Chinese American identity.
It is funny and messy, and not without its structural flaws. But the questions it asks of Hwang and the audience make it both a rollicking and thought-provoking evening.
Yellow Face doesn’t fire on all cylinders but one can’t deny its relevance to contemporary concerns.
The strident tone, vapid observations and clunky structure, render this play as unfunny and not very interesting.
The ridiculousness of this scenario keeps the audience laughing throughout the taut, 90-minute show.
Provocative and clever, Yellow Face raises excellent questions on bias and perception, with particular attention to questions like “where are you really from?”

cn.t: Hwang's smart, funny meta-theatrical satire about identity and casting politics earns widespread praise for its sharp wit and continued relevance, though some find its self-examination more defensive than incisive.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'

vr.q: I love this play... still applicable still an interesting discussion... I may even go back and see this play again
this play is funny, pointed, unapologetic — describeable in a lot of ways that I feel are quite subversive to Asian stereotypes. And I love subversion.
